title: How Do Pastors Fight Comparison and Envy in Ministry?
subtitle: Why comparison and envy among pastors poisons ministry joy, how metrics and the other man's larger church feed the discontent, and the only cure that frees a leader to rejoice at another's success.

sections.title: Comparison Is the Thief That Wears a Collar
sections.body:
It rarely arrives looking like sin. It arrives looking like ambition, or excellence, or a healthy desire to grow. You see the other man's church, the numbers, the building, the platform, the book deal, and something tightens in your chest that you would never name out loud.

You would not call it envy. You would call it being challenged. But it does not produce gratitude or growth. It produces a low ache, a discontent with the very work God gave you, a quiet inability to be glad about your own people because they are not as many or as impressive as his.

Comparison does not make you better. It makes you bitter, and it does it slowly, while you tell yourself you are only paying attention to the field.

sections.title: The Tyranny of the Scoreboard
sections.body:
We have built a ministry culture that runs on metrics. Attendance, giving, baptisms, followers, downloads. None of it is evil on its own. All of it becomes a tyrant the moment it becomes the scoreboard that tells you whether you matter.

The problem is that God never gave you those numbers to measure yourself by. He gave you a charge to be faithful, and faithfulness does not always show up on a chart. The man planting in hard soil may labor a lifetime for fruit he never sees. The man in the easy soil may grow fast and shallow. The scoreboard cannot tell the difference, and the leader who lives by it will despair in the lean years and grow proud in the fat ones.

When David numbered the people, it was counted against him as sin. There is a way of counting that is really a way of trusting yourself instead of God.

sections.title: Envy Says God Was Wrong to Bless Him
sections.body:
Strip envy down and look at what it actually believes. It believes that God made a mistake when He blessed the other man. It resents the gift because the gift went to someone else. It cannot rejoice with those who rejoice because it secretly thinks the rejoicing should have been ours.

This is why envy rots the bones, as Proverbs says. It is corrosive at the deepest level, because it sets a man against the providence of God. It makes you an accuser of the divine arrangement, unable to celebrate a brother's harvest without feeling robbed of your own.

I have felt it. I have heard of a friend's growing church and had to fight to be glad. The fight itself told me the truth about my heart, and it was not flattering.

sections.title: Tend Your Own Garden and Bless His
sections.body:
Jesus dealt with this directly. When Peter looked at John and asked what about him, Jesus said what is that to you. You follow me. The cure for comparison is not to win the comparison. It is to stop running the race against the other man and start running the one set before you.

God did not call you to his ministry. He called you to yours. Tend the garden He actually gave you, with the soil He actually provided, and stop measuring your rows against the man across the valley. And when his garden flourishes, bless it, out loud, until your heart catches up to your words, because the ability to rejoice at a brother's success is one of the surest signs that envy has lost its grip.

Your faithfulness is the only thing God will ask you about. Not your size. Not his.

sections.title: Joy Returns When the Comparing Stops
sections.body:
Here is the mercy on the far side of repentance. When the comparing stops, the joy comes back. The people in front of you become precious again instead of insufficient. The small wins become real wins again instead of disappointments measured against someone else.

Comparison is the thief of ministry joy. Kill it, and the joy it stole comes home. You will find you actually love these people, this place, this work, the moment you stop wishing it were a different one.

Follow Him. What the other man has is between God and the other man. You have a flock to love. Go love it, gladly.
